core: Dynamics as the analysis of bodies that accelerate, and its division into kinematics and kinetics
Rectilinear versus curvilinear motion of a particle
Projectile motion as two independent one-dimensional problems, with the neglect-drag idealization named and bounded
Normal and tangential components of acceleration, and the fact that a curved path produces a normal (centripetal) component even at constant speed
Circular motion and the centripetal force requirement; centrifugal force as an artifact of a rotating frame rather than a force in an inertial frame
Relative motion and the choice of reference frame; the velocity addition relation
Rigid-body rotation about a fixed axis: angular position, angular velocity, angular acceleration, and v = omega r
Moment of inertia as rotational inertia and its dependence on how mass is distributed about the axis

claims.claim: Dynamics divides into kinematics — the study of motion in space and time without considering the forces that cause it — and kinetics, the study of motion in relation to mass and forces; kinetics relates forces to accelerations and the equation of motion, while kinematics relates that equation and the constraint equations to the actual motion.

Motions along perpendicular axes are independent and can be analysed separately, which is why projectile motion is treated as constant-velocity horizontal motion (a_x = 0) plus constant-acceleration vertical motion (a_y = -g); the treatment explicitly neglects air resistance, and for launch and landing at the same height the range is R = v0^2 sin(2*theta0)/g, maximised at 45 degrees.

Aerodynamic drag depends on air density, the square of the velocity, viscosity, compressibility, and the size, shape and inclination of the body, and is collected into D = Cd * rho * V^2 * A / 2, with Cd almost always determined experimentally; this is why the drag-free idealization degrades as speed rises.

A particle moving along a curved trajectory has non-zero acceleration even when its speed is constant; in uniform circular motion the acceleration has magnitude a_c = v^2/r and points toward the centre of the circle.

In normal-tangential coordinates the acceleration of a particle on a plane curve is a = (dv/dt) u_t + (v^2/rho) u_n, where rho is the radius of curvature of the path at that point and the two components are perpendicular, so the total acceleration is their vector sum.

Centripetal force is not a new kind of force but the net force requirement F_c = m v^2 / r that any combination of real forces — tension, gravity, friction, normal force — must supply to hold a body on a circular path; for an ideally banked curve tan(theta) = v^2/(r g), independent of vehicle mass.

Centrifugal force does not exist as a force in an inertial frame; it is a fictitious inertial force that appears only when motion is described in a rotating (non-inertial) frame, as is the Coriolis force.

Velocity is always stated with respect to a reference frame and transforms by v_PS = v_PS' + v_S'S; if the relative velocity of the two frames is constant then their relative acceleration is zero and both observers measure the same acceleration.

For rotation about a fixed axis, angular position relates to arc length by theta = s/r, angular velocity is omega = d(theta)/dt in rad/s, angular acceleration is alpha = d(omega)/dt in rad/s^2, the tangential speed of a point at radius r is v = omega r, and every point on the rigid body shares the same omega.

Moment of inertia I = sum of m_j r_j^2 (units kg*m^2) is the quantitative measure of rotational inertia, the rotational counterpart of mass; the greater the moment of inertia the greater the resistance to a change in angular velocity, and mass placed farther from the axis contributes more than the same mass placed close to it. For a uniform thin disk about its central axis I = (1/2) m R^2, and the parallel-axis theorem gives I = I_cm + m d^2.

For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis the net torque equals the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration, sum of tau = I alpha; in engineering-dynamics form the pair of equations is sum F = m a and sum M = I alpha, moments may be taken about the axis of rotation O or the centre of mass G provided the moment and the mass moment of inertia are taken about the same point, and in balanced rotation (centre of mass on the axis) the centre of mass has zero acceleration.

Standard engineering dynamics organises the kinetics of both point masses and rigid bodies into three parallel method families — the direct force/moment-acceleration equations, work and energy, and impulse and momentum (angular impulse and momentum for rigid bodies) — and textbooks provide explicit solution strategies for choosing among them.

Worked-example arithmetic, executed with python3: for a uniform disk flywheel m = 12.0 kg, R = 0.250 m, I = 0.5 * 12.0 * 0.250^2 = 0.375 kg*m^2; a 18.0 N belt force at the rim gives M = 18.0 * 0.250 = 4.50 N*m; alpha = 4.50 / 0.375 = 12.0 rad/s^2; 300 rev/min = 300 * 2*pi/60 = 31.4159 rad/s; t = 31.4159 / 12.0 = 2.617994 s, reported as 2.62 s. Check: (1/2)*alpha*t^2 = 41.1234 rad and omega^2/(2*alpha) = 41.1234 rad agree to 7e-15 rad, i.e. 6.54 revolutions. Unit check: N*m / (kg*m^2) reduces to s^-2.

Question-bank arithmetic, executed with python3: 25.0^2 / 125 = 5.00 m/s^2 centripetal; sqrt(2 * 20.0 / 9.81) = 2.019275 s, so 12.0 * 2.019275 = 24.2313 m, reported as 24.2 m (the no-square-root error gives 12.0 * 4.0775 = 48.9 m and the halving error gives 12.1 m); 0.375 * 8.00 = 3.00 N*m, with 0.375/8.00 = 0.046875 and 8.00/0.375 = 21.33 as the inverted distractors.

The value 9.81 m/s^2 used in the projectile arithmetic is a rounded working value for local free-fall acceleration; the exact defined standard acceleration of gravity is g_n = 9.806 65 m/s^2, and local g varies with position, so results carrying it are reported to three significant figures at most.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether 'centrifugal force' is a legitimate term.
positions: Introductory physics treatment: centrifugal force does not exist; it is a fictitious inertial force arising only in a rotating reference frame.
Working engineering usage: 'centrifugal force' is used loosely for the outward reaction a rotating part exerts on its restraint, and for the d'Alembert inertial term in a rotating-frame formulation.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the inertial-frame position as the correction — in an inertial frame there is no outward force on the body, only an inward net force — and separately acknowledges that a rotating frame legitimately carries an inertial term, so students recognise the working usage without adopting the misconception. Sourced to OpenStax University Physics 6.3, which states the point explicitly.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which value of g to use in the projectile arithmetic.
positions: g_n = 9.806 65 m/s^2 exactly, the defined conventional standard.
9.81 m/s^2, the conventional three-figure working value.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Used 9.81 m/s^2 and stated in the lesson that it is a rounded working value, with results reported to three significant figures. The exact defined value is recorded from the NIST fundamental-constants page.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive claims about dynamics at all — its body text was subject-agnostic filler ('Dynamics is a concept students use to organize information') that named no equation, no variable, and no idealization.
The draft's vocabulary entries ('context', 'evidence', 'application') were generic and circular and had no relationship to dynamics.
The draft's Eli-10 analogy ('a label on a toolbox drawer') carried no mechanical content and had no stated limits.
correctionsNeeded: Discarded the generated draft entirely and wrote the lesson from verified sources.
Established the kinematics/kinetics split as the organising frame, which the draft did not mention.
Added the constant-speed-implies-zero-acceleration misconception and the centrifugal-force correction to Common Mistakes, both of which the draft lacked.
Named the neglect-of-drag idealization explicitly and bounded it with the NASA drag equation rather than presenting projectile formulas as unconditional.
Added the required educational-material and not-design-guidance statements per the subject source-map caution.
Replaced the placeholder worked example with a fixed-axis rotation problem whose every number was executed with python3 and which carries an independent consistency check.
Raised estimatedMinutes from 8 to 13 to match the actual content.
rightsIssues: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1 is openly licensed, but the per-book licence terms were not independently verified for this project, so all OpenStax pages are held at REFERENCE_ONLY and no OpenStax wording was reproduced or paraphrased.

The LibreTexts Mechanics Map pages carry a stated CC BY-SA 4.0 licence and the LibreTexts Introductory Dynamics (Steeneken) pages carry a stated CC BY 4.0 licence, both read from the page footers. Even so, both are held at REFERENCE_ONLY here because no text, figure, or example from either was adapted — only facts were taken and the prose is original.

The NASA Beginner's Guide to Aeronautics page is U.S. government work; it was read via curl because the WebFetch client could not verify the host's certificate chain. Only the drag equation's form and its stated dependence on the square of velocity were used.
No engineering standard (ASME, ASTM, ISO, AISC, ACI, IEEE) was consulted, quoted, or relied on, and no allowable stress, load factor, or design value appears anywhere in the lesson.
